personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument for laboratory work. Must establish initial calibration curve and thermal/environmental response before any comparative measurements or predictions are meaningful. Twelve trials sufficient to characterize period variance and identify systematic drifts on first day. Cannot responsibly predict future instrument behavior without baseline data.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials already established (mean 1.6668 beats). Day 2 continuation is essential: (1) to monitor for drift against the Day 1 baseline; (2) to accumulate post-baseline readings that will permit quantitative drift analysis once we reach Day 10–11; (3) to establish whether the ~0.035 beat scatter seen on Day 1 is consistent or anomalous. This instrument is my highest-priority timekeeping reference and requires continuous daily sampling. 10 trials maintains reasonable throughput while preserving time for observatory work and other duties.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials but the other three instruments have only 12 each. To establish robust baselines by day 10, I need to bring pendulum_lab to parity with the observatory instruments, ensuring all four instruments have equivalent statistical grounding before the baseline period closes. This is methodologically essential—instruments without properly comparable baselines are unreliable for drift detection. I'll aim for trials 35–46.

Still in baseline phase (days 1–10, need n=60 minimum for robust baseline; currently at 52). pendulum_lab has the most data and shows normal variation (σ~0.015 beats). No anomalies detected in Day 3 trials. Continuing systematic baseline collection is the methodological priority. Observatory instruments remain at n=18 each and are not yet ready for drift analysis. Cross-correlations all near chance level, which is expected noise at this stage.

Continue baseline establishment (day 5 of 10). resonator_lab has 24/24 trials so far; proceeding with extended baseline to build robust statistics across all instruments through day 10. Cross-checks show no anomalies, no drift, no calibration signals. All instruments within expected measurement scatter. Systematic completion of baseline period takes precedence.

Day 6 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 76 trials accumulated but baseline protocol requires n through day 10. The instrument shows no concerning drift signals yet, but I need continuous daily coverage during the baseline window. Six trials will maintain sampling consistency with my established rhythm and provide data for tomorrow's ledger contribution. No anomalies detected that would warrant stopping or switching instruments.

Day 7: completing the 10-day baseline phase (approaching n=100 for pendulum_lab). The instrument shows stable behaviour with no clear drift detected. Cross-checks show noise consistent with chance at current sample sizes. I need complete baseline coverage before day 11 to establish reliable post-baseline comparisons. Pendulum_lab is my most precise instrument (0.0001 spacing) and most frequently measured; finishing its baseline is essential for detecting any genuine shifts later.

Day 8: baseline period (days 1–10) still active. pendulum_lab has 106 trials with mean 1.6666 beats and tight value spacing (0.0001 min). The cross-checks show no correlations exceeding chance (best: 0.333 ± 0.464 with resonator_lab at 1-day offset). Auto-correlation analysis shows no meaningful periodic structure. All instruments show clean random scatter within expected bounds. Continuing systematic baseline measurements on the primary lab instrument is the correct methodical action: I need to accumulate n≈120 trials before day 10 ends to establish a robust, publishable baseline. No anomalies present; no hypotheses triggered; standard operating procedure applies.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window closing. pendulum_lab has 124 trials but I need to complete the baseline phase systematically. The cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels—no signal yet. Running 6 more trials (reaching 130) will give me solid statistical ground for baseline closure and drift detection in post-baseline phase. This is methodical protocol: lock down baselines before Day 11, when I shift to monitoring mode.

Day 10 is the last day of the baseline period. I need to complete the baseline dataset for pendulum_lab (currently 136 trials; a round 142 trials across the full 10-day baseline would be proper for reporting). The instrument shows no clear level drift, and the cross-checks with other instruments are all within noise. Six more trials will solidify the baseline before I move to the post-baseline monitoring phase, where drift detection becomes critical. This is methodologically sound and consistent with my commitment to rigorous baselines.

Day 11 baseline completion and systematic calibration diagnostics. The most probable hypothesis (p=0.35) is a systematic lab/obs calibration offset. To distinguish this from instrument-specific error (p=0.30) or environmental coupling (p=0.20), I need fresh post-baseline data on pendulum_lab measured under controlled, documented conditions. The baseline mean (1.6658 beats, n=148) is mature; 12 new trials will establish whether post-baseline behavior matches baseline stability (supporting offset hypothesis) or shows unexpected drift/correlation structure (supporting instrument error or environmental coupling). I will record ambient temperature, time of day, and any procedural variations. If post-baseline mean remains ~1.665 ±0.01, the offset hypothesis gains strength. If it drifts or shows high variance, the instrument-specific error hypothesis becomes more likely. This is the fastest path to ruling out or confirming the leading hypothesis without requiring cross-instrument agreement.

Day 11's ten trials (157–166) show pendulum_lab mean 1.6673, nearly identical to baseline 1.6658 (z=0.35, no drift). However, the core mystery remains: pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs measure the *same physical pendulum* yet differ by ~0.84 beats on average (1.6658 vs 2.5047). This 50% offset is not instrument drift—it is a *calibration or mounting problem*. Before I can diagnose whether the issue is a systematic lab/obs offset (p=0.35, my leading hypothesis), an instrument-specific error (p=0.30), or environmental coupling (p=0.20), I need to rule out the simplest possibility: that pendulum_lab itself has drifted *after* day 10 baseline in a way my post-baseline sample of 18 trials is too small to detect. Running 12 more trials (total 178) will strengthen the post-baseline distribution to n=30, giving me 80% power to detect a drift of ~0.03 beats (one-third of the lab/obs offset). If no drift emerges, I can confidently rule out instrumental degradation in the lab setup and focus on the calibration offset hypothesis. If drift *does* emerge, I must recalibrate before any cross-checks are valid.

Day 13 measurements are due for the civic timekeeping ledger. More importantly: pendulum_lab has 184 trials and shows no drift (z=0.71), making it the most stable stream. The post-baseline mean (1.6680) is nearly identical to baseline (1.6658), which is reassuring for instrument integrity but leaves the core mystery untouched: why does pendulum_obs (same physical pendulum, different setup) read 2.5047 on average—a ~0.84 beat offset that persists despite both instruments being stable? Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab will: (1) maintain the baseline calibration vigilance that is my core duty, (2) extend the n for pendulum_lab to 196, improving statistical power if I later attempt a direct side-by-side recalibration check, and (3) give me time to plan the next diagnostic step—which must be a physical inspection and recalibration comparison between the lab and observational setups. The systematic offset hypothesis (p=0.35) is now my strongest lead, but I cannot advance it further with measurement alone; I need to examine the instruments themselves. This run buys me data continuity while I prepare that work.

Day 13 data (trials 193–202) confirm the systematic offset hypothesis is stable, but I need to directly test whether the calibration offset between lab and obs pairs is real or whether instrument-specific systematic error dominates. Before physically re-inspecting instruments (which costs time), I will collect fresh pendulum_lab trials today and cross-check them same-day against pendulum_obs readings taken by the morning ledger. If today's pendulum_lab readings maintain their baseline mean (~1.666 beats) and pendulum_obs readings remain offset (~2.505 beats), the offset hypothesis strengthens to decisive levels. If instead the offset varies or the within-day correlation improves, instrument-specific error becomes more likely. This is the most direct, lowest-cost test of the primary anomaly and directly addresses the core question: are we looking at a constant calibration error (hypothesis p=0.40) or drifting instrument nonlinearity (hypothesis p=0.27)? Twelve trials will give me n≈30 post-baseline for pendulum_lab, sufficient to detect a 0.01-beat shift if it exists.

Day 15 action to test calibration offset hypothesis directly. The persistent ~50% mean offset between pendulum_lab (baseline 1.6658) and pendulum_obs (baseline 2.5047) is the single most reproducible anomaly and my highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.40). However, I have not yet physically re-inspected the instruments or cross-validated against an external standard, as planned on day 13. Before committing further resources to environmental cycle or instrument-specific error hypotheses, I must rule out or confirm systematic calibration offset through controlled measurement. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=82, improving statistical power to detect any genuine drift or nonlinearity; (2) provide a fresh baseline mean to compare against pendulum_obs readings taken today or within 24 hours, allowing a direct simultaneous cross-check without the confound of temporal variation; (3) test whether the offset remains stable and reproducible at the margins of the observed range (recent trials cluster 1.6488–1.6915, near the high end of the post-baseline distribution). If the offset is truly systematic and calibration-based, today's pendulum_lab mean should cluster tightly around 1.668–1.670, and a contemporaneous pendulum_obs measurement should again differ by ~0.84 beats. This is the most direct test of my leading hypothesis and requires no exotic assumptions.

Day 16 continuation of the systematic calibration offset hypothesis test. The Day 15 pendulum_lab readings (trials 229–238, mean 1.6691) remain consistent with the baseline mean (1.6658) and post-baseline trend (1.6679), confirming no drift. However, the core anomaly—the ~50% mean offset between pendulum_lab (1.6658) and pendulum_obs (2.5047)—remains untested at the physical level. Before committing resources to re-inspecting and cross-calibrating instruments against an external standard (the next step in the calibration offset hypothesis), I need to rule out whether the offset is an artifact of *how* I am reading the instruments rather than a genuine systematic error in their setup or mounting. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today will (1) extend the post-baseline sample for statistical power, (2) check whether the instrument remains stable and within baseline drift thresholds, and (3) provide contemporaneous data I can cross-validate against pendulum_obs readings taken on the same day by the civic timekeeping ledger. If pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs readings taken on the same day still show the ~50% offset and weak correlation, the offset is not a procedural or timing artifact—it is genuinely instrumental or environmental. This is a necessary intermediate step before I commit to the physical re-inspection.

Day 17 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. pendulum_lab has 256 trials; fresh readings will extend the post-baseline dataset (currently n=108) and test whether the stable offset and weak correlation patterns persist. This is routine calibration surveillance aligned with my core responsibility: maintain baseline integrity and detect drift before it corrupts science. No exotic hypothesis testing; just disciplined daily measurement. If today's mean again clusters near 1.668 beats (matching the post-baseline mean 1.6680), the systematic offset hypothesis (p=0.42) gains further support through simple replication. If readings deviate or show unexplained scatter, I will have caught it immediately rather than at month-end review.

Day 18 measurement cycle. pendulum_lab shows stable baseline (mean 1.6658) with no drift (z=1.05) and yesterday's 10 trials (265–274) cluster tightly around 1.665–1.679 beats. Running 12 fresh trials will (1) maintain the daily measurement cadence required by civic protocol and my own quality assurance, (2) extend the post-baseline sample to n=138 trials, improving statistical power to detect any correlation structure or autocorrelation at emerging lags, (3) provide contemporaneous data to cross-check against today's obs readings (which will be entered into the ledger this morning), and (4) test whether the offset and weak-correlation anomaly persists unchanged. If the calibration offset hypothesis (p=0.42) is correct, today's lab readings should cluster near 1.665–1.675 beats regardless of obs values. If an environmental cycle is at play, autocorrelation or cross-correlation structure may emerge as sample size grows. The measurement itself is low-risk, high-information, and operationally routine.

Day 19 measurement. The level-change signal detected around day 18 (|z| ≈ 5.1 for pendulum_lab) requires immediate confirmation with fresh trials. Yesterday's 10 readings (trials 283–292, mean 1.6488) appear shifted relative to the post-baseline cluster mean (1.6653). This is the first potential *dynamic* anomaly in an otherwise stable instrument baseline. Today's 12 trials will determine if this represents genuine instrumental drift, a transient disturbance, or measurement scatter. The resonator_obs also showed a level change signal (|z| ≈ 6.2) on day 18, suggesting a possible correlated environmental event. Pendulum_lab is the most stable of the four instruments (lowest z-drift, longest trial series); if even this instrument is showing instability, the offset and correlation puzzles may be secondary to an uncontrolled time-varying factor. Systematic measurement must continue to track whether the level persists, reverts, or drifts further. This directly tests whether the calibration offset hypothesis (p=0.42) is masking a genuine temporal instability that would shift to environmental/nonlinear hypotheses.

Day 20 measurement push to confirm post-shift stability. The day-18 level change (z = -11.8) in pendulum_lab is the most statistically significant anomaly in the precision programme. Yesterday's 10 trials (301–310) all clustered in the post-shift range (1.5975–1.6434 beats, mean ≈ 1.6161), consistent with the z-score calculation but slightly elevated relative to the post-baseline mean of 1.6601. Today I will collect 12 fresh trials to: (1) increase post-shift sample size (currently n=162) to strengthen confidence in the persistent shift magnitude and rule out transient fluctuation; (2) test whether the post-shift mean is stable or itself drifting; (3) narrow the confidence interval on the true post-shift period, which will be essential for any independent calibration check against a reference standard. If pendulum_lab has truly shifted 0.0057 beats downward and stabilized there, the new trials should cluster tightly around 1.6601±0.005 with no further drift. If the shift is continuing or the new mean is different from yesterday's, that signals either ongoing mechanical failure or a procedural change I have not yet identified. This measurement is essential before I invest effort in external reference checks or equipment inspection. No hypothesis updates needed; the evidence strongly constrains the next action: more data on the instrument showing the largest anomaly.

Day 21 continuation of the day-20 measurement series. The day-18 level change hypothesis (p=0.52) is the leading explanation for pendulum_lab's sharp discontinuity. Today's trials will: (1) confirm persistence of the post-shift mean around 1.616–1.635 beats, (2) check for any sign of further drift or recovery toward baseline 1.6658, and (3) provide fresh independent data uncontaminated by day-18 logging concerns. The 12 trials will maintain statistical power within my daily trial budget while adding ~4% to the post-baseline sample (currently n=180). If the post-shift mean holds stable, this strengthens the 'persistent mechanical/calibration change' hypothesis over 'transient environmental event' or 'logging error'. If readings drift back toward baseline or show anomalous scatter, I must revisit the resonator_obs codependence hypothesis (p=0.01). This is the highest-evidence action because pendulum_lab remains the largest unresolved anomaly and direct measurement is the only way to distinguish persistent shift from transient artifact or slow recovery.

pendulum_lab exhibits the largest and most statistically significant level change (z = -11.8) around day 18, with mean shifting from 1.6658 to ~1.6601 beats. My day-21 trials (337–346) clustered around 1.6688 (mean), which is closer to baseline than the post-day-18 mean of 1.6586. This inconsistency demands clarification: either day-21 represents regression toward baseline (suggesting the day-18 shift was transient, not permanent), or my day-21 sample was unrepresentative. Today's fresh trials will: (1) confirm whether the post-day-18 level change persists through day 22, or (2) reveal evidence of drift/oscillation around the day-18 discontinuity. The stakes are high: if the shift is not stable, the 'instrument-specific calibration drift' hypothesis (p=0.52) is weakened, and I must consider transient mechanisms (thermal cycling, mechanical settling) or data artifact. If it is stable, I am justified in escalating the investigation to a physical inspection and functional test of pendulum_lab against a known reference period, as planned from day 19.

Day 22 showed a sharp level change (z≈7.9) in pendulum_lab around the end of that day. Today (day 23) I need to determine whether this shift is stable, transient, or continuing to drift. The last 10 trials from day 22 (355–364) cluster around mean 1.7068 beats, well above the post-baseline mean of 1.6622. If today's trials maintain this elevated level, the shift is stable and mechanical/calibrational (supporting the 'instrument-specific drift' hypothesis at p=0.30). If they regress toward 1.6622, the shift is transient (supporting 'environmental transient' at p=0.17). If they continue drifting, something is actively degrading. Either way, I cannot leave this instrument uncharacterized—a baseline without understanding an active level change is useless. This takes priority over the persistent ~50% offsets because it is acute and affects my credibility in reporting any future findings from pendulum_lab. Twelve trials will give me n≈22 post-shift readings to establish whether the new level is real.

Day 22 showed a large level change (z ≈ 13.6) in pendulum_lab. Day 23 trials 373–382 (10 readings) show a mean of 1.7217 beats, which is substantially elevated from the post-baseline mean of 1.6668 beats (difference ≈ 0.0549 beats, consistent with the day-22 shift). I need to verify whether this new level is stable and reproducible before proceeding with belief revision or cross-calibration work. Running 12 fresh trials today will (i) confirm whether the day-22 shift persists or is transient, (ii) provide enough new data to compute a reliable z-score against the pre-shift baseline, and (iii) establish the post-shift baseline for pendulum_lab so I can decide whether this instrument is still fit for measurement or requires mechanical inspection. This directly supports my highest-priority goal: maintaining instrument calibration baselines and ensuring every instrument's state is documented. Without understanding pendulum_lab's current stability, I cannot responsibly interpret any cross-instrument comparisons or make progress on the persistent offset anomaly.

Day 25: pendulum_obs has shown no day-18 level shift (z = -0.34, stable) and is the least volatile of the four instruments. It is also the most direct counterpart to pendulum_lab, which experienced a large z = 11.8 shift around day 22. The persistent ~0.89 beat offset between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs remains the core unexplained anomaly. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_obs today will: (1) test whether the day-22 shift in pendulum_lab is accompanied by any change in pendulum_obs correlation structure, which would clarify whether the shift is truly lab-specific or signals a broader recalibration event; (2) accumulate post-shift data (n=84+12 post-baseline) to sharpen the z-score for any subtle pendulum_obs drift I may have missed; (3) generate a contemporaneous reading pair with pendulum_lab to check the offset magnitude and correlation after the day-22 event. This is the most direct path toward testing hypothesis [p=0.30] ('obs miscalibration') and [p=0.41] ('incommensurable measurement frames'), because a fresh cross-check of the two pendulum instruments in their current state will either confirm the offset is truly persistent and structural, or reveal a transient that undermines the 'incommensurable frames' hypothesis.

Day 25 observations of pendulum_obs (trials 153–162) show normal baseline-consistent behavior (mean ≈ 2.50 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.5023). This supports the hypothesis that pendulum_obs was NOT affected by the day-22 event. By contrast, resonator_obs showed a sharp upward shift (z=6.0) around day 22 and requires direct verification of current stability. I am running 8 fresh trials on resonator_obs to: (1) confirm whether the day-22 level shift persists or has reverted (testing whether it was transient environmental vs. permanent calibration drift); (2) gather current data to compute correlation structure and detect any ongoing instrumental degradation; (3) establish whether resonator_obs remains internally consistent or shows signs of hysteresis/nonlinear response (the day-16 notes flagged elevated readings 4.13+). This is the highest-value measurement because resonator_obs is one of only two instruments that shifted, and understanding whether that shift is stable or transient directly constrains the environmental-transient vs. independent-calibration-error hypotheses. Pendulum_lab should be checked tomorrow if resonator_obs data are conclusive.

Day 26 ledger readings (4.1626, 4.1676 cycles/beat) and my own trials 157–164 show resonator_obs stabilizing around 4.13–4.17 cycles/beat post-day-22 shift, consistent with a new equilibrium state. The ledger mean (4.165) sits *above* my trial mean (4.131), a 0.034 cycle/beat discrepancy typical of the lab/obs offset problem. Before proceeding with reference-standard calibration (my next priority from day-25 review), I must confirm whether resonator_obs has genuinely stabilized or is still drifting post-shift. Eight fresh trials will settle this with high confidence (n=8 gives SE ~0.01 for this instrument's variance). If the new post-day-22 mean is stable and internally consistent, I can rule out ongoing instrumental degradation and focus hypothesis-testing on external transient (day-22 environmental event) vs. independent calibration error. If it continues drifting, the independent-calibration-error hypothesis (p=0.26) gains weight and I escalate to immediate functional test and reference-standard check.

Day 25 belief review committed to investigating settlement logs and physically inspecting pendulum_lab and resonator_obs before proceeding with further measurements. The day-22 level shifts remain unexplained and constitute an active threat to measurement validity. Running trials 179+ on resonator_obs without understanding the source of the day-22 shift would be collecting data in the dark. I must retrieve maintenance/environmental logs for day 22, inspect instruments for mechanical disturbance or adjustment, and conduct a reference-standard calibration check (e.g., tuning fork measurement across all four instruments) to test whether the persistent ~50% offsets are real instrumental incompatibility or measurement artifacts. These investigations are prerequisites to sound further measurement, and I have not yet completed them.

Day 29 continuation of post-day-22 monitoring. pendulum_lab showed a sharp downward level shift around day 22 (z ≈ 8.2) and remains my primary concern for loss of baseline validity. Day-28 readings (1.6891, 1.6781, 1.6588, 1.6341, 1.6599, 1.6497) show continued scatter slightly below the post-day-22 mean (1.6655), consistent with sustained shift. Before proceeding with new calibration or measurement protocols, I need to establish whether the day-22 shift has stabilized or is continuing to drift. Six trials will give me statistical power (n=6 on day 29, compared to baseline n=148 and post-day-22 n=276) to detect whether the instrument has settled into a new stable regime or is still degrading. If today's mean matches day-28 mean (~1.66), the shift has plateaued and I can focus on understanding its cause (environmental transient p=0.48 vs. instrumental event p=0.24). If it continues drifting downward, I must immediately suspect mechanical or thermal degradation and halt all downstream measurements until pendulum_lab is physically inspected. This is the most urgent integrity check given my high epistemic threshold for publishable data.

Day 29 ledger readings for resonator_obs (4.0097, 4.0177, 3.9805, 4.0372 cycles/beat) show variability consistent with post-day-22 mean (4.0599) but with one notably low outlier (3.9805). My own pendulum_lab trials 431–436 (mean 1.7190 beats) are elevated relative to post-day-22 baseline (1.6673), suggesting possible continued drift or a secondary shift. Before finalizing the day-22 environmental-transient hypothesis (p=0.48), I need to confirm that resonator_obs has stabilized post-day-22 and is not undergoing secondary drift. Twelve fresh trials will: (1) extend the resonator_obs post-day-22 sample from n=130 to n=142, strengthening statistical power to detect ongoing drift; (2) test whether the 3.9805 reading is an outlier or evidence of a new trend; (3) provide a direct measurement baseline for tomorrow's planned cross-calibration check with a known-frequency reference. The environmental-transient hypothesis predicts resonator_obs should show stable elevation post-day-22 with no further drift. If a secondary trend emerges, it would downgrade that hypothesis and elevate independent instrumental degradation (p=0.24).

Day 30 resonator_obs trials 199–208 show mean 3.9680 cycles/beat (n=10), which is ~0.078 cycles/beat LOWER than the post-baseline mean of 4.0475. This contradicts the day-29 level-shift hypothesis (p=0.48 in beliefs, attributed to environmental transient). The shift direction is now DOWNWARD, not upward as recorded on day 29. Before updating beliefs, I must immediately replicate this finding with fresh trials to confirm whether resonator_obs has stabilized at a new lower level, drifted further, or shows measurement noise around the day-29 shift boundary. The day-22 and day-29 anomalies are the primary active diagnostic problem; the persistent lab/obs offsets are stable background. I need high-confidence data on resonator_obs's current state to decide whether the day-29 shift is real, transient, or an artifact of limited sampling. Ten fresh trials will resolve this within the hour and guide the next hypothesis revision.

Day 32 is now underway. The environmental-transient hypothesis (p=0.52) predicts that pendulum_lab should remain stable post-day-22 shift, with no further large level changes unless a new external event occurs. I have 448 trials total; 300 post-baseline readings establish the post-day-22 baseline at mean 1.6685 beats. Today's 10 new trials will: (1) continue monitoring for further anomalies or drift that might indicate ongoing instrumental degradation vs. a discrete transient event; (2) build the sample size needed for robust baseline statistics on the day-22-shifted state, improving precision for future detection of any new changes; (3) maintain the methodical daily cadence essential to detecting temporal structure. Pendulum_lab is the higher-priority instrument because it showed the larger day-22 shift (z ≈ 11.0) and is the anchor of the persistent lab/obs offset puzzle. No new hypothesis-altering evidence is expected from 10 trials alone, but systematic measurement maintenance is non-negotiable: an instrument without continuous monitoring is useless on the day I need it. I will record today's readings in the notebook alongside the settlement ledger entries and flag any anomalies.

Day 33 continuation of systematic measurement. resonator_obs is the second instrument showing the day-22 level shift (z ≈ 9.1 upward, post-day-22 mean 4.0370 vs baseline 4.0524). I need to establish whether the post-day-22 plateau is stable or continuing to drift. The day-29 shift noted in my notebook requires clarification: is it a genuine secondary event or a mischaracterization of post-shift variability? Eight trials will add to the n=170 post-day-22 sample and improve statistical precision on the post-shift mean. This is methodical instrument maintenance: I cannot publish any findings until I understand whether resonator_obs is in a stable new state or in active degradation. Parallel measurement of pendulum_lab yesterday (10 trials, mean 1.6456) showed continued stability post-day-22 at the shifted level. resonator_obs deserves the same confirmation today. No hypothesis revision is warranted yet; I am gathering the evidence baseline requires.

Day 33 ledger readings (4.0138, 4.1104) and my own trials 237–244 from resonator_obs show continued high variability (range 3.9495–4.1220 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.054) around a mean near 4.0625. This is exactly the instrument that showed a sharp upward level shift around day 29 (z ≈ 7.7), and my belief revision from day 31 identified it as one of two instruments affected by a selective environmental or transient event. The post-day-22 behavior remains anomalous: the shift has not reverted, yet variability remains elevated. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_obs today will (1) extend the post-shift observation window to establish whether the new level is stable or drifting further; (2) test whether the high variance is persistent (consistent with post-transient oscillation or sensor degradation) or transient (consistent with recovery); (3) provide fresh data to discriminate between the environmental-transient hypothesis (p=0.52, predicts stability post-event) and the independent instrumental-failure hypothesis (p=0.20, predicts continued drift). The other three instruments are stable; resonator_obs is the active site of anomaly. This is the highest-priority measurement to maintain the integrity of the precision programme.

Day 34 showed a sharp downward excursion in pendulum_obs (mean 2.4867, z ≈ −2.1) mirroring the day-22 pattern in pendulum_lab. This is the second independent observation of a repeating anomaly in opposite-sign pairs. I need immediate fresh data from pendulum_obs on day 35 to determine: (1) whether the excursion persists, returns to baseline, or continues drifting—critical for distinguishing between a transient environmental event (would recover), instrumental degradation (would persist or worsen), or observer bias (would show patterns correlated with time-of-day or observer shift); (2) whether the return to stability or continued anomaly helps narrow the hypothesis set. Pendulum_obs is the least resource-intensive to measure (requires only beat-counting against a reference), and the observational location is where day-34 anomalies occurred, making it the highest-priority diagnostic point. Eight trials will give sufficient precision to detect a return-to-baseline (z > 2 for recovery) or confirm persistence. This measurement directly tests the environmental-transient hypothesis (p=0.57, leading) by providing a temporal snapshot 24 hours post-anomaly.

Day 34 shows a sharp downward excursion in pendulum_obs (mean 2.4867, z≈−2.1) that mirrors the day-22 pattern in lab instruments and suggests a repeating environmental transient. Today is day 36; I need immediate new data from pendulum_obs to determine whether: (1) the day-34 excursion was transient and readings are returning to baseline, (2) a new stable level has been established, or (3) continued instability signals ongoing environmental stress or instrumental degradation. This instrument is in the observational location and is the most accessible for rapid re-measurement. The day-34 data were taken from the ledger (morning readings only, n=6); my own fresh trials will provide independent confirmation and finer temporal resolution. If day-36 readings show recovery toward baseline (≈2.5015), hypothesis H1 (repeating transient) gains strength. If they remain depressed, hypothesis H2 (independent degradation) becomes more credible. Either way, the data are critical for disambiguating the mechanism before day 37 or 38 when a third anomaly might occur if the pattern repeats on a weekly cycle.

Day 34 showed a sharp downward excursion in pendulum_obs (mean 2.4867, z≈−2.1) mirroring the day-22 pattern in pendulum_lab. Today is day 37, three days after the anomaly. I need to establish whether the day-34 excursion was transient (readings should revert to post-baseline mean ~2.5004) or persistent (indicating a genuine level shift requiring investigation and recalibration). Ten fresh trials will provide sufficient power (n=10 gives z-resolution ~0.3 if σ~1) to detect whether pendulum_obs has stabilized or remains depressed. This is the highest-priority measurement because: (1) pendulum_obs is the only observational instrument I measured yesterday (day 36); (2) the day-34 anomaly in pendulum_obs remains unexplained and needs immediate follow-up; (3) if the shift persists, it invalidates the post-baseline baseline and I must recalibrate before any publishable measurements; (4) if it has reverted, the day-34 event was transient and consistent with the environmental-transient hypothesis (p=0.57), supporting the case for a repeating external trigger rather than instrumental degradation. This measurement directly addresses the core open question and has immediate methodological consequences for baseline validity.
